t.2.79.1: Thus addressed, the greatly wise Bharata replied to Guha, lord of the Niṣādas, with words full of reason and meaning.
t.2.79.3: Having spoken thus to Guha, the illustrious and greatly radiant Bharata again addressed excellent words to the lord of the Niṣādas.
t.2.79.2: Noble indeed is your wish, O friend of my elder, and it is as good as fulfilled, since you alone desire to honor such a great army for my sake.
t.2.79.4: By which way shall I go to the hermitage of Bharadvāja, O Guha? This region is exceedingly dense, a marshy tract along the Gaṅgā, hard to pass through.
t.2.79.5: Having heard those words of the wise prince, Guha, who roamed the deep forests, spoke these words with joined palms.
t.2.79.6: The fishermen, armed with bows and fully alert, will follow you, and I too will follow, O prince of great renown.
t.2.79.7: I hope you are not going with ill intent toward Rāma, whose deeds are untiring? This great army of yours seems to stir suspicion in me.
t.2.79.8: To Guha, who was speaking thus, Bharata, pure as the clear sky, spoke these words in a gentle voice.
t.2.79.9: May that time never come, for it would be a grievous thing! You ought not to suspect me, for that Rāghava is my elder brother, equal to my father.
t.2.79.10: I am going to bring back that Kākutstha who dwells in the forest. You should not think otherwise, O Guha; I tell you the truth.
t.2.79.11: But he, his face beaming with joy, having heard what Bharata had said, spoke once more to Bharata, delighted.
t.2.79.12: Blessed are you; I see no one equal to you on the face of the earth, you who here wish to renounce a kingdom that has come to you without effort.
t.2.79.13: Your fame will surely be everlasting and will travel through all the worlds, since you wish to bring back Rāma, who has fallen into hardship.
t.2.79.14: As Guha was thus speaking to Bharata, the sun, its radiance lost, shone dimly, and night came on.
t.2.79.15: Having settled that army in camp, the glorious one, gratified by Guha, went back to his bed together with Śatrughna.
t.2.79.16: Such grief, born of anxious thought for Rāma, had indeed come upon the great-souled Bharata, who did not deserve it and whose eyes were ever fixed on dharma.
t.2.79.17: A fire, burning within, torments the Rāghava, as a hidden fire torments a tree already scorched by a forest blaze.
t.2.79.18: Sweat born of the fire of grief streamed from all his limbs, just as the Himavān, scorched by the rays of the sun, streams with melting snow.
t.2.79.19: By a mountain whose caverns were brooding thought, whose ores were his deep sighs, whose clustered trees were dejection, and whose towering peaks were sorrow, weariness and anguish.
t.2.79.20: The son of Kaikeyī was crushed beneath a great mountain of sorrow, whose countless creatures were bewilderment and whose herbs and bamboos were burning anguish.
t.2.79.21: Bharata, of great nobility, came together with Guha, accompanied by his people and composed in mind. Then Guha, himself deeply downcast, once more consoled that Bharata concerning his elder brother.
